topics.title: Osmosis, osmotic pressure and reverse osmosis
topics.summary: Semipermeable membranes, osmosis, the equation for osmotic pressure, isotonic solutions in medicine, and desalination by reverse osmosis.

lessons.title: Osmosis and osmotic pressure
lessons.objective: Define osmosis and osmotic pressure, predict the direction of solvent flow, and use $\pi = CRT$ (choosing the right units of $R$) to find an osmotic pressure or a molar mass.

blocks.text: Raw mangoes shrivel in brine, wilted flowers revive in fresh water, and blood cells collapse in salty water. In each case a **membrane** separates two liquids. Membranes such as pig's bladder, parchment or synthetic cellophane have submicroscopic pores: small solvent molecules (water) pass through, bigger solute molecules are held back. These are **semipermeable membranes (SPM)**.

blocks.title: Definitions
blocks.text: **Osmosis**: the flow of solvent molecules through a semipermeable membrane from pure solvent to the solution (or from a dilute to a more concentrated solution). Solvent always flows from lower to higher solute concentration. **Osmotic pressure**: ==the excess pressure that must be applied to a solution to prevent osmosis==, i.e. to stop the passage of solvent molecules through a semipermeable membrane into the solution.

blocks.title: Why does the solvent move that way?
blocks.text: On the pure-solvent side every particle hitting the membrane is a solvent particle. On the solution side some of the surface is taken up by solute particles, so fewer solvent particles cross back per second. More cross into the solution than out of it - a net flow towards the side with more solute.

blocks.caption: Solvent enters the thistle funnel through the membrane and the level of the solution rises (NCERT Fig. 1.9). Applying a pressure equal to the osmotic pressure on the solution side stops the flow (Fig. 1.10).
blocks.alt: Thistle funnel with solution, closed by a semipermeable membrane, dipping in water

blocks.label: Osmotic pressure (dilute solutions)
blocks.where: $C$ = **molarity**; $V$ = volume of solution in litres; $R$ = 0.083 L bar mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ (or 0.0821 L atm mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$). Osmotic pressure is colligative: it depends on the number of solute particles, not their identity.
symbols: mass and molar mass of solute
blocks.conditions: Dilute solutions. Note that this one uses **molarity** (volume of solution), unlike $\Delta T_b$ and $\Delta T_f$, which use molality. For electrolytes multiply by $i$.

blocks.title: Choosing the value of R
blocks.text: Pick $R$ so that its units match the pressure you want and the volume you have. Pressure in **atm**, volume in L: $R$ = 0.0821 L atm K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$. Pressure in **bar**, volume in L: $R$ = 0.083 L bar K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$. Pressure in **Pa**, volume in m$^3$: $R$ = 8.314 J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$ (1 J = 1 Pa m$^3$). Always use the value the question gives.

blocks.title: Molar mass of a protein
blocks.problem: 200 cm$^3$ of an aqueous solution contains 1.26 g of a protein. Its osmotic pressure at 300 K is $2.57 	imes 10^{-3}$ bar. Find the molar mass.
blocks.why: Osmotic pressure is the colligative property that gives the amount of solute; the mass then turns that into a molar mass.

convert.why: $R$ is per litre, so the volume must be in litres.

convert.t: Pressure is in bar, so take $R$ = 0.083 L bar K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$
convert.why: The units of $R$ must match the pressure unit so that bar cancels.

blocks.check: Proteins are large molecules, so a molar mass of tens of thousands is expected - and the tiny osmotic pressure is still measurable, which is why this method is used.

blocks.title: Why osmotic pressure is the method of choice for proteins and polymers
items: Pressure is measured around **room temperature** - biomolecules are generally not stable at higher temperatures.
It uses **molarity** instead of molality.
Its magnitude is **large even for very dilute solutions**, so it can be measured accurately when $\Delta T_b$ or $\Delta T_f$ would be tiny - polymers have poor solubility.
Osmosis: solvent flows through an SPM towards the side with more solute.
Osmotic pressure: the extra pressure on the solution that stops osmosis.
$\pi = CRT$ with molarity; match $R$'s units to the pressure unit; $T$ in kelvin.

lessons.title: Isotonic solutions and reverse osmosis
lessons.objective: Classify solutions as isotonic, hypertonic or hypotonic, predict what happens to cells, and explain reverse osmosis and desalination.

blocks.text: **Isotonic solutions** have the ==same osmotic pressure at a given temperature==; separated by a semipermeable membrane, no osmosis occurs between them. The fluid inside blood cells is isotonic with **0.9% (mass/volume) NaCl** - **normal saline**, safe to inject intravenously.

left.title: Hypertonic (more than 0.9% NaCl)
items: Higher osmotic pressure than the cell fluid
Water flows **out** of cells: they **shrink**
Raw mango in brine shrivels into pickle

right.title: Hypotonic (less than 0.9% NaCl)
items: Lower osmotic pressure than the cell fluid
Water flows **into** cells: they **swell** (and may burst)
Wilted flowers and limp carrots firm up in fresh water; raisins swell in water

blocks.title: Isotonic glucose and urea solutions
blocks.problem: What mass percentage (w/V) of urea (60 g mol$^{-1}$) is isotonic with a 5% (w/V) glucose (180 g mol$^{-1}$) solution at the same temperature?
given: Glucose 5 g per 100 mL, $M$ = 180 g mol$^{-1}$
blocks.relation: Isotonic → equal $\pi$ → equal $CRT$ → equal molarity (same $T$, same $i$).
blocks.why: With $R$ and $T$ the same on both sides, equal osmotic pressure simply means equal concentration of particles.
blocks.check: Urea's molar mass is one-third of glucose's, so one-third of the mass gives the same number of particles: 5/3 = 1.67.

blocks.title: More osmosis in daily life (NCERT)
items: Eating a lot of salt causes water retention in tissue cells and intercellular spaces - the puffiness is called **edema**.
Water moving from soil into plant roots and upwards is partly due to osmosis.
Meat is preserved by salting and fruit by sugar: a bacterium on salted meat or candied fruit loses water by osmosis, shrivels and dies.

blocks.text: If a pressure ==larger than the osmotic pressure== is applied on the solution side, the flow reverses: pure solvent is pushed out of the solution through the membrane. This is **reverse osmosis**, used for **desalination of sea water**. The pressure needed is high. A workable membrane is a film of **cellulose acetate** on a support - permeable to water, impermeable to impurities and ions in sea water.

blocks.caption: Schematic after NCERT Fig. 1.11: a pressure larger than the osmotic pressure on the sea-water side drives water out through the membrane; the salts stay behind. Not to scale.
blocks.alt: Container split by a membrane; a piston presses on the sea water side and water moves to the fresh water side

blocks.text: 2026 case study (osmosis passage) asked: amount of CaCl$_2$ ($i$ = 2.59) for $\pi$ = 0.70 atm, raisins swelling (osmosis), why osmotic pressure is advantageous, and desalination (reverse osmosis). 2025 asked RBCs in 0.5% NaCl (they swell - hypotonic) and to name an SPM for reverse osmosis (cellulose acetate).

items: Isotonic = same osmotic pressure; 0.9% (w/V) NaCl is isotonic with blood cells.
Hypertonic outside → cells shrink; hypotonic outside → cells swell.
Reverse osmosis: pressure greater than $\pi$ on the solution side; cellulose acetate membrane; desalination.

topics.title: Abnormal molar masses and the van't Hoff factor
topics.summary: What happens to colligative properties when a solute dissociates or associates, the van't Hoff factor, and the degree of dissociation and association.

lessons.title: Abnormal molar masses and the van't Hoff factor
lessons.objective: Explain why dissociation and association give abnormal molar masses, define the van't Hoff factor in three equivalent ways, and predict $i$ for common solutes.

blocks.text: Colligative properties count particles. If a solute **dissociates**, there are more particles than formula units; if it **associates**, fewer. The measured colligative property then gives a molar mass that is wrong - an **abnormal molar mass**: ==a molar mass that is either lower or higher than the expected or normal value==

left.title: Dissociation (KCl in water)
items: 1 mol KCl gives 1 mol K$^+$ + 1 mol Cl$^-$: 2 mol particles
Expected $\Delta T_b$ for 1 m KCl ≈ 2 × 0.52 = 1.04 K
Experimental molar mass comes out **lower** than the true value (about 37.25 instead of 74.5 g mol$^{-1}$)

right.title: Association (ethanoic acid in benzene)
items: Molecules dimerise by **hydrogen bonding**, which happens in solvents of low dielectric constant: $\ce{2CH3COOH <=> (CH3COOH)2}$
Particles are halved, so $\Delta T_f$ or $\Delta T_b$ is about half the normal value
Experimental molar mass comes out **higher** (about twice) the true value

blocks.title: van't Hoff factor, $i$ (1880)
blocks.text: $i = \dfrac{	ext{normal molar mass}}{	ext{abnormal molar mass}} = \dfrac{	ext{observed colligative property}}{	ext{calculated colligative property}} = \dfrac{	ext{total moles of particles after association/dissociation}}{	ext{moles of particles before association/dissociation}}$. Abnormal molar mass is the experimentally determined one; the calculated colligative property assumes the solute neither associates nor dissociates.

items: $i > 1$: dissociation. $i < 1$: association. $i = 1$: neither (glucose, urea, sucrose).
Aqueous KCl: $i$ close to 2. Ethanoic acid in benzene: $i$ nearly 0.5.

For complete dissociation $i$ = number of ions per formula unit: NaCl, KCl 2; CaCl$_2$, Na$_2$SO$_4$, K$_2$SO$_4$, MgBr$_2$ 3; AlCl$_3$ 4; Al$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$ 5. For CaCl$_2 \cdot$6H$_2$O the water of crystallisation does not count: $i$ = 3.

blocks.caption: NCERT Table 1.4: $i$ approaches the ideal value as the solution becomes very dilute
head: Salt
0.1 m

Complete dissociation

blocks.title: Why is $i$ for NaCl less than 2?
blocks.text: Counting 2 particles per NaCl assumes each ion moves independently. In a real solution oppositely charged ions attract and some stay close together, so they act like fewer particles. On dilution the ions are farther apart, this effect weakens and $i$ approaches 2. The whole-number value is an **idealised particle count**.

blocks.title: van't Hoff factor from an abnormal molar mass
blocks.problem: Freezing-point measurements on an aqueous KCl solution give an experimental molar mass of 40.2 g mol$^{-1}$. The formula mass of KCl is 74.5 g mol$^{-1}$. Find $i$ and the degree of dissociation.
blocks.relation: $i$ = normal ÷ abnormal molar mass; for $n$ ions, $i = 1 + (n-1)\alpha$.
blocks.why: Dissociation makes more particles, so the colligative property is larger and the molar mass calculated from it is smaller than 74.5.
blocks.check: $i$ is between 1 and 2, as expected for partial dissociation into two ions.

items: Dissociation → $i > 1$ → molar mass appears smaller. Association → $i < 1$ → appears larger.
$i$ = normal $M$ / observed $M$ = observed / calculated colligative property.
Whole-number $i$ (2, 3, 4 …) assumes complete dissociation and independent ions.
blocks.next: Lesson 9.2: putting $i$ into the equations, and comparing solutions.

lessons.title: Using $i$ in calculations, and comparing solutions by $i 	imes m$
lessons.objective: Include $i$ in all four colligative equations, and rank solutions by freezing point, boiling point or osmotic pressure using $i 	imes$ concentration - stating when molarity can stand in for molality.

blocks.label: Colligative equations with $i$
blocks.tex: rac{p_1^\circ - p_1}{p_1^\circ} = i\, rac{n_2}{n_1}, \quad \Delta T_b = i K_b m, \quad \Delta T_f = i K_f m, \quad \pi =  rac{i\,n_2 RT}{V}
blocks.conditions: Dilute solutions. With a measured $i$ these describe real behaviour; with a whole-number $i$ they assume complete dissociation and independent ions (an idealised particle count).

blocks.text: The size of each colligative effect is set by the **concentration of particles**. For freezing and boiling points that is $i 	imes m$ (molality); for osmotic pressure it is $i 	imes C$ (molarity). The larger $i 	imes m$, the larger the depression - so the **lower** the freezing point and the **higher** the boiling point.

blocks.caption: Ranking 0.1 mol kg$^{-1}$ aqueous solutions (complete dissociation assumed)
head: Solute
$i$
$i 	imes m$ / mol kg$^{-1}$
$\Delta T_f = 1.86\,i\,m$ / K

blocks.title: Three assumptions behind the shortcuts
blocks.text: (1) **Molarity for molality.** Many questions give '0.1 M' for a freezing-point comparison. $\Delta T_f$ needs molality; for dilute **aqueous** solutions 1 L of solution is close to 1 kg of water, so M ≈ m and the ranking is unaffected. (2) **Whole-number $i$.** Real values are a little smaller (NCERT Table 1.4), but rarely enough to change a ranking between solutes with different ion counts. (3) **Equal masses, not equal moles.** If the solutions are equal in **mass %**, compare particles per gram, $i/M$, not $i$ alone (2025: 1% CaCl$_2$, 3/111, just beats 1% KCl, 2/74.5).

blocks.title: Ranking by freezing point
blocks.problem: Arrange in order of increasing freezing point: 0.10 m glucose, 0.10 m NaCl, 0.05 m CaCl$_2$ (all aqueous; assume complete dissociation).
blocks.find: Order of freezing points, lowest first.
blocks.relation: $\Delta T_f = iK_fm$: same solvent, so $\Delta T_f \propto i 	imes m$.
blocks.why: Comparing $i 	imes m$ avoids calculating each value; $K_f$ is the same for all three because the solvent is the same.

calc.t: Largest $i 	imes m$ → largest depression → lowest freezing point: NaCl < CaCl$_2$ < glucose

blocks.check: Note the trap: CaCl$_2$ has the largest $i$ but only half the molality, so NaCl wins.
blocks.answer: Increasing freezing point: 0.10 m NaCl < 0.05 m CaCl$_2$ < 0.10 m glucose

items: Multiply by $i$ in every colligative equation.
Rank by $i 	imes m$ (freezing/boiling) or $i 	imes C$ (osmotic pressure).
M ≈ m only for dilute aqueous solutions; for equal mass %, compare $i/M$.

lessons.title: Degree of dissociation and association
lessons.objective: Derive $i = 1 + (n-1)\alpha$ and $i = 1 - \alpha/2$, and use them to find the percentage dissociation or association from colligative data.

blocks.label: Dissociation into $n$ ions (degree $\alpha$)
blocks.where: e.g. AB $	o$ A$^+$ + B$^-$: $n$ = 2, so $\alpha = i - 1$. Used in the CBSE marking schemes.
blocks.conditions: Exact particle bookkeeping: start with 1 mol, $\alpha$ mol dissociate into $n\alpha$ mol of ions, $1 - \alpha$ mol stay whole. Total $= 1 - \alpha + n\alpha$.

blocks.label: Association into dimers (degree $\alpha$)
blocks.conditions: Start with 1 mol of A; $\alpha$ mol associate into $\alpha/2$ mol of dimers; $1 - \alpha$ mol stay single.

blocks.title: Association of benzoic acid
blocks.problem: 2 g of benzoic acid ($\ce{C6H5COOH}$) in 25 g of benzene depresses the freezing point by 1.62 K. $K_f$(benzene) = 4.9 K kg mol$^{-1}$. What is the percentage association if it forms a dimer?
given: Normal molar mass of C$_6$H$_5$COOH = 122 g mol$^{-1}$
blocks.relation: Experimental $M_2$ from $\Delta T_f$; then $i$ = normal/experimental; then $\alpha = 2(1 - i)$ for a dimer.
blocks.why: Association makes the measured molar mass too large; the ratio to the true molar mass gives $i$.
blocks.check: The experimental molar mass is almost exactly twice 122, so nearly all molecules have dimerised.

blocks.title: Dissociation of acetic acid in water
blocks.problem: 0.6 mL of acetic acid (density 1.06 g mL$^{-1}$) in 1 L of water depresses the freezing point by 0.0205 °C. Find $i$ and the dissociation constant.
given: 0.6 mL acetic acid, density 1.06 g mL$^{-1}$, $M$ = 60 g mol$^{-1}$
blocks.relation: $i$ = observed $\Delta T_f$ ÷ calculated $\Delta T_f$; for HA → H$^+$ + A$^-$, $\alpha = i - 1$; $K_a = c\alpha^2/(1 - \alpha)$.
blocks.why: Comparing the observed depression with the one expected for no dissociation gives $i$ directly.

convert.why: Density turns the volume of acid into its mass.

blocks.check: Acetic acid is a weak acid, so only about 4% dissociation and a $K_a$ near $10^{-5}$ are expected.

blocks.text: The association problem has appeared in almost every recent year: 5 g benzoic acid in 35 g benzene, $\Delta T_f$ = 2.94 K (2020, 2023, 2025, 2026 compartment); 0.3 g acetic acid in 30 g benzene (2023, 2025); benzoic acid in CS$_2$ dimerising 88% (2026); benzoic acid by osmotic pressure (2023).

In association problems, molality uses the **normal** molar mass (122 for benzoic acid). Then multiply by $i < 1$. Do not use the dimer's molar mass and $i$ together - that counts the association twice.

items: Dissociation: $\alpha = (i - 1)/(n - 1)$.
Dimer association: $\alpha = 2(1 - i)$.
Use the normal molar mass in the molality, then $i$.

questions.q: Find the osmotic pressure of a 0.050 M aqueous urea solution at 300 K. ($R$ = 0.0821 L atm K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$)

mistakes.msg: You used 27 (°C) for the temperature. In $\pi = CRT$ the temperature must be in kelvin.
Check the concentration: 0.050 mol L$^{-1}$ is already per litre - do not convert it again.

hints: Substitute into $\pi = CRT$ with $T$ in kelvin.

questions.q: The molar mass of NaCl found from the osmotic pressure of its aqueous solution is 31.5 g mol$^{-1}$. Find the van't Hoff factor. (NaCl = 58.5 g mol$^{-1}$)

scaffold.t: Normal molar mass = 58.5 g mol$^{-1}$; observed (abnormal) = 31.5 g mol$^{-1}$

mistakes.msg: You divided observed by normal. $i$ = normal molar mass ÷ observed molar mass, and for a dissociating salt it must be more than 1.

hints: $i = \dfrac{	ext{normal molar mass}}{	ext{abnormal molar mass}}$.

questions.q: Find the freezing point of a 0.10 m aqueous CaCl$_2$ solution, assuming complete dissociation. ($K_f$ = 1.86 K kg mol$^{-1}$; water freezes at 273.15 K.)

mistakes.msg: That is the freezing point without the van't Hoff factor. CaCl$_2$ gives 3 ions, so multiply by $i$ = 3.
You used $i$ = 2. CaCl$_2$ gives one Ca$^{2+}$ and **two** Cl$^-$: $i$ = 3.

hints: How many ions does one CaCl$_2$ give?
$\Delta T_f = 3 	imes 1.86 	imes 0.10$; subtract from 273.15 K.

questions.q: Benzoic acid (122 g mol$^{-1}$) dimerises in benzene. Its experimental molar mass from a freezing-point measurement is 240 g mol$^{-1}$. Find the percentage association.

mistakes.msg: That is $1 - i$. For dimerisation $i = 1 - \alpha/2$, so $\alpha = 2(1 - i)$.
